        <span style="flex: 1;">
          <span style="display: block; font-size: 0.7rem; font-weight: 700; color: #F97316; text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: 1.5px; margin-bottom: 4px;">Issue #4 &bull; 20 May 2026</span>
          <span style="display: block; font-size: 1rem; font-weight: 700; color: #F8FAFC;">A semester-end check-in</span>
        </span>
        <span style="color: #64748B; font-size: 1.2rem; flex-shrink: 0;">&#9662;</span>

      <div style="padding: 0 20px 16px 52px;">
        <div style="font-size: 0.95rem; color: #94A3B8; line-height: 1.7; margin-bottom: 12px;">
          Rather than another AI focused piece, I want to use this issue to ask a question and offer some options for AI Facilitation within SoMM.
        </div>

        <div style="font-size: 0.85rem; color: #CBD5E1; line-height: 1.6; padding-top: 12px; border-top: 1px solid #2D2D4A;">
          <strong style="color: #F8FAFC;">What is already there</strong><br><br>
          The AI Skills Passport has grown steadily through semester 1. If you have not had time to look, here is a quick orientation. Note that to meet Curtin&rsquo;s data governance and privacy you will need to be logged into Blackboard (done by visiting a Curtin Blackboard site). So even though it does not look like it, this is a Blackboard site.<br><br>
          <strong style="color: #F8FAFC;">Arrivals Hall:</strong> the hub that links everything below. If you have not been to the Passport before, <a href="https://lms.curtin.edu.au/bbcswebdav/orgs/The_AI_Skills_Passport/arrivals-hall.html" target="_blank" style="color: #F97316; text-decoration: underline;">start here</a>.<br><br>
          <strong style="color: #F8FAFC;">AI Toolkit:</strong> a searchable library of practical frameworks, templates, and one-pagers. <a href="https://lms.curtin.edu.au/bbcswebdav/orgs/The_AI_Skills_Passport/ai-toolkit.html" target="_blank" style="color: #F97316; text-decoration: underline;">Browse the full collection</a>.<br><br>
          <strong style="color: #F8FAFC;">Experiences:</strong> short, role-relevant interactive pieces on detection, ethics, policy, assessment design, and working with AI. <a href="https://lms.curtin.edu.au/bbcswebdav/orgs/The_AI_Skills_Passport/experiences.html" target="_blank" style="color: #F97316; text-decoration: underline;">Browse the experiences</a>.<br><br>
          <strong style="color: #F8FAFC;">AI in 5:</strong> a five-minute challenge each week, voluntary and low-pressure. <a href="https://forms.office.com/r/3531YvKVeg?origin=lprLink" target="_blank" style="color: #F97316; text-decoration: underline;">Subscribe</a> if you would like one each week.<br><br>
          <strong style="color: #F8FAFC;">Past Briefings:</strong> every issue, <a href="https://lms.curtin.edu.au/bbcswebdav/orgs/The_AI_Skills_Passport/the-briefing-archive.html" target="_blank" style="color: #F97316; text-decoration: underline;">archived here</a>.
        </div>

        <div style="font-size: 0.85rem; color: #CBD5E1; line-height: 1.6; padding-top: 12px; margin-top: 12px; border-top: 1px solid #2D2D4A;">
          <strong style="color: #F8FAFC;">What might come next for AI Facilitation?</strong><br><br>
          The following are ideas, not announcements. Tell me which would be useful and semester 2 will be shaped accordingly:<br><br>
          &bull; A short, hands-on workshop on assessment redesign for a specific unit, course, or School<br><br>
          &bull; One-on-one scoping help with an AI problem you are wrestling with (an assessment, a research workflow, a professional process)<br><br>
          &bull; A bespoke tool or small app for something you do repeatedly. I have built a few of these for colleagues now and they are usually faster than people expect<br><br>
          &bull; A live conversation session, in person or on Teams, on one topic for an hour. Here are some ideas: AI in the trough of disillusionment (a business school read on the cycle), teaching AI use to students who are still learning their domain or field, AI and research integrity, or whatever you would actually like an hour on<br><br>
          &bull; More of something already in the Skills Passport that you found useful
        </div>

        <div style="font-size: 0.85rem; color: #CBD5E1; line-height: 1.6; padding-top: 12px; margin-top: 12px; border-top: 1px solid #2D2D4A;">
          Email <a href="mailto:michael.borck@curtin.edu.au" style="color: #F97316; text-decoration: underline;">michael.borck@curtin.edu.au</a>, or reply to the email version of this Briefing if you got it that way. One line is fine. &ldquo;I would use X&rdquo; or &ldquo;I would not use Y but I wish you would do Z&rdquo; are both genuinely useful.<br><br>
          The Briefing itself goes quiet for a while, returning in week 2 of semester 2 with whatever shape this round of replies generates.<br><br>
          The inter-semester gap is a good window for the bespoke options listed above: an assessment you want to redesign, a unit you are reshaping, a small tool you want built, a research workflow you want to tidy before teaching resumes.

    <details style="background: #16162A; border: 1px solid #2D2D4A; border-radius: 10px; margin-bottom: 12px;">
      <summary style="padding: 16px 20px; cursor: pointer; list-style: none; display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 12px;">
        <span style="font-size: 1.3rem; flex-shrink: 0;">&#129504;</span>
        <span style="flex: 1;">
          <span style="display: block; font-size: 0.7rem; font-weight: 700; color: #F97316; text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: 1.5px; margin-bottom: 4px;">Issue #3 &bull; 6 May 2026</span>
          <span style="display: block; font-size: 1rem; font-weight: 700; color: #F8FAFC;">The question is whether the thinking converges too</span>
        </span>
        <span style="color: #64748B; font-size: 1.2rem; flex-shrink: 0;">&#9662;</span>
      </summary>
      <div style="padding: 0 20px 16px 52px;">
        <div style="font-size: 0.95rem; color: #94A3B8; line-height: 1.7; margin-bottom: 12px;">
          A paper worth your attention: Sourati et al., &ldquo;The homogenizing effect of large language models on human expression and thought,&rdquo; <em>Trends in Cognitive Sciences</em>, 2026. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tics.2026.01.003" target="_blank" style="color: #F97316; text-decoration: underline;">https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tics.2026.01.003</a>
        </div>

        <div style="font-size: 0.85rem; color: #CBD5E1; line-height: 1.6; padding-top: 12px; border-top: 1px solid #2D2D4A;">
          <strong style="color: #F8FAFC;">Worth reading</strong><br><br>
          When millions of people use the same handful of models to write and reason, output flattens. Language converges. Reasoning styles collapse toward a single dominant template.<br><br>
          After LLM polishing, you can no longer reliably tell from text whether the author is young or old, or where they sit politically. Adjusting temperature or persona prompting doesn&rsquo;t fix it.<br><br>
          Participants who co-wrote with opinionated models mirrored the model&rsquo;s stance and then shifted their own opinions in subsequent attitude surveys. They adopted the framing without realising it.<br><br>
          Groups of people who reason differently consistently outperform groups of the highest-ability individuals. In creative ideation experiments, LLM-assisted participants generated more ideas individually but produced semantically similar outputs across the group. AI made individuals more productive and made the collective less diverse.
        </div>

        <div style="font-size: 0.85rem; color: #CBD5E1; line-height: 1.6; padding-top: 12px; margin-top: 12px; border-top: 1px solid #2D2D4A;">
          <strong style="color: #F8FAFC;">Something worth thinking about</strong><br><br>
          Sourati et al. give structural explanation to findings accumulating separately: Shaw and Nave on cognitive surrender, Kosmyna et al. on weaker neural engagement, Fan et al. on metacognitive laziness.<br><br>
          The technology will keep converging. The question is whether the thinking does too.
        </div>

        <div style="font-size: 0.85rem; color: #CBD5E1; line-height: 1.6; padding-top: 12px; margin-top: 12px; border-top: 1px solid #2D2D4A;">
          <strong style="color: #F8FAFC;">From the AI Toolkit</strong><br><br>
          One frame for resisting the pull toward the average: the Question Architect (type &lsquo;question&rsquo; in search). When AI makes answers cheap, the scarce skill is knowing what to ask and why the answer matters. Domain knowledge isn&rsquo;t made redundant by AI &mdash; it&rsquo;s what stops AI output from being noise.
        </div>
      </div>
    </details>

    <details style="background: #16162A; border: 1px solid #2D2D4A; border-radius: 10px; margin-bottom: 12px;">
      <summary style="padding: 16px 20px; cursor: pointer; list-style: none; display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 12px;">
        <span style="font-size: 1.3rem; flex-shrink: 0;">&#129309;</span>
        <span style="flex: 1;">
          <span style="display: block; font-size: 0.7rem; font-weight: 700; color: #F97316; text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: 1.5px; margin-bottom: 4px;">Issue #2 &bull; 22 Apr 2026</span>
          <span style="display: block; font-size: 1rem; font-weight: 700; color: #F8FAFC;">AI literacy is about strategies, not tools</span>
        </span>
        <span style="color: #64748B; font-size: 1.2rem; flex-shrink: 0;">&#9662;</span>
      </summary>
      <div style="padding: 0 20px 16px 52px;">
        <div style="font-size: 0.95rem; color: #94A3B8; line-height: 1.7; margin-bottom: 12px;">
          Khan Academy&rsquo;s Khanmigo was one of the most talked-about AI tools in education. A <a href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/2026/04/09/sal-khan-reflects-on-ai-in-schools-and-khanmigo/" target="_blank" style="color: #F97316; text-decoration: underline;">recent article</a> has Sal Khan reflecting on what Khanmigo delivered.
        </div>

        <div style="font-size: 0.85rem; color: #CBD5E1; line-height: 1.6; padding-top: 12px; border-top: 1px solid #2D2D4A;">
          <strong style="color: #F8FAFC;">Worth reading</strong><br>
          His verdict: for many students it was &ldquo;a non-event. They just didn&rsquo;t use it much.&rdquo; His own chief learning officer was blunter still: &ldquo;So far I am not seeing the revolution in education.&rdquo;<br><br>
          His diagnosis is simple but easy to miss. Students lacked the foundational knowledge to ask the tool useful questions. And even those who could use it often didn&rsquo;t, because nobody was prompting them to. He used the analogy of a skilled human tutor sitting in the corner of a classroom: some students will seek them out, most won&rsquo;t.<br><br>
          His conclusion: &ldquo;I think our biggest lever is really investing in the human systems.&rdquo;
        </div>

        <div style="font-size: 0.85rem; color: #CBD5E1; line-height: 1.6; padding-top: 12px; margin-top: 12px; border-top: 1px solid #2D2D4A;">
          <strong style="color: #F8FAFC;">Something worth thinking about</strong><br>
          That same dynamic shows up elsewhere. In teaching, it might be students who have access to AI tools but not yet the conceptual grounding to use them well. In research, it might be having enough clarity about what you&rsquo;re investigating to ask AI something meaningful. In any team, it might be whether anyone is actively building the habits and context for AI use, or whether the tool is just sitting in the corner.<br><br>
          Think about an AI tool you or your colleagues can already access. What&rsquo;s the human system around it &ndash; or is there one?
        </div>

        <div style="font-size: 0.85rem; color: #CBD5E1; line-height: 1.6; padding-top: 12px; margin-top: 12px; border-top: 1px solid #2D2D4A;">
          <strong style="color: #F8FAFC;">From the AI Toolkit</strong><br>
          A practical frame for thinking about where to bring AI in and where to hold back: the toolkit has a resource on the <a href="https://lms.curtin.edu.au/bbcswebdav/orgs/The_AI_Skills_Passport/downloads/ai-last-resort-philosophy.html" target="_blank" style="color: #F97316; text-decoration: underline;">AI-as-last-resort philosophy</a>. Start with what needs to happen, then ask whether AI adds something genuine at each step. Strategy first, tool second.<br><br>
          Browse the full toolkit: <a href="https://lms.curtin.edu.au/bbcswebdav/orgs/The_AI_Skills_Passport/ai-toolkit.html" target="_blank" style="color: #F97316; text-decoration: underline;">The AI Toolkit</a>.
        </div>
      </div>
    </details>

    <details style="background: #16162A; border: 1px solid #2D2D4A; border-radius: 10px; margin-bottom: 12px;">
      <summary style="padding: 16px 20px; cursor: pointer; list-style: none; display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 12px;">
        <span style="font-size: 1.3rem; flex-shrink: 0;">&#128221;</span>
        <span style="flex: 1;">
          <span style="display: block; font-size: 0.7rem; font-weight: 700; color: #F97316; text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: 1.5px; margin-bottom: 4px;">Issue #1 &bull; 08 Apr 2026</span>
          <span style="display: block; font-size: 1rem; font-weight: 700; color: #F8FAFC;">Assessment in the age of AI</span>
        </span>
        <span style="color: #64748B; font-size: 1.2rem; flex-shrink: 0;">&#9662;</span>
      </summary>
      <div style="padding: 0 20px 16px 52px;">
        <div style="font-size: 0.95rem; color: #94A3B8; line-height: 1.7; margin-bottom: 12px;">
          With the upcoming L&amp;T Seminar, this fortnight&rsquo;s feature is on assessment.
        </div>

        <div style="font-size: 0.85rem; color: #CBD5E1; line-height: 1.6; padding-top: 12px; border-top: 1px solid #2D2D4A;">
          <strong style="color: #F8FAFC;">Worth attending</strong><br>
          Sonia and Claire&rsquo;s L&amp;T Seminar Series has a session coming up that will interest anyone thinking about assessment design. Sam Cholayil is presenting on practical strategies for designing AI-resilient assessments. Rather than detection or prohibition, the focus is on authenticity and equity. You&rsquo;ll work with a real assessment task during the session.<br><br>
          Wednesday 22 April, 12:00 to 1:00 pm, Room 402.216. Face-to-face, BYOD.
        </div>

        <div style="font-size: 0.85rem; color: #CBD5E1; line-height: 1.6; padding-top: 12px; margin-top: 12px; border-top: 1px solid #2D2D4A;">
          <strong style="color: #F8FAFC;">Something worth thinking about</strong><br>
          Traditional assessments tend to have convergent outputs. An essay question has a finite space of good answers. A programming spec has a narrow set of correct solutions. That convergence is what makes collusion easy and tempting. Two students can share work because their work was always going to look similar anyway.<br><br>
          What if we assessed the pathway instead? Two students can arrive at identical outputs via completely different pathways, one having learned deeply and one having learned nothing. Traditional assessment measures the destination. Assessing the journey is a fundamentally more honest picture of whether learning happened. And there are lots of ways of assessing the journey, from AI conversation, to documenting and cross-referencing papers, websites, journals etc. Think of the learning journey as field notes to the final report.
        </div>

        <div style="font-size: 0.85rem; color: #CBD5E1; line-height: 1.6; padding-top: 12px; margin-top: 12px; border-top: 1px solid #2D2D4A;">
          <strong style="color: #F8FAFC;">From the AI Toolkit</strong><br>
          The AI Skills Passport toolkit has an <a href="https://lms.curtin.edu.au/bbcswebdav/orgs/The_AI_Skills_Passport/downloads/stress-test-prompt-sequence.html" target="_blank" style="color: #F97316; text-decoration: underline;">Assessment AI Stress Test</a> you can run against any of your assessments in about 15 minutes. It&rsquo;s a prompt sequence, not an app, by design, so you retain human agency. You see exactly what&rsquo;s being asked, you can modify prompts on the fly, and you&rsquo;re never just ratifying an output you didn&rsquo;t follow. The AI is the analyst. You are the assessor.<br><br>
          The toolkit also has resources on assessment strategy (individual and group), rubric design, and more. Browse it anytime: <a href="https://lms.curtin.edu.au/bbcswebdav/orgs/The_AI_Skills_Passport/ai-toolkit.html" target="_blank" style="color: #F97316; text-decoration: underline;">The AI Toolkit</a>.<br><br>
          Also worth a look is Curtin&rsquo;s own <a href="https://staffportal.curtin.edu.au/learning-and-teaching/assessment-2030/" target="_blank" style="color: #F97316; text-decoration: underline;">Assessment 2030</a> for some ideas.
        </div>
      </div>
    </details>
